content: Dr. Ben Croxford from University College London conducted a calculation in 2001 at the request of a journalist. He estimated the weight of particulate matter inhaled during cigarette smoking and compared it to the time required in the most polluted part of the London Underground to inhale an equivalent weight of particulate matter. However, this calculation did not consider the health effects of cigarette smoke versus underground dust. It was purely a comparison of the weight of inhaled particles. Cigarette smoke contains harmful substances such as combustion byproducts (carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur oxides), alkaloids, aromatic hydrocarbons, and tar. In contrast, the dust in the London Underground primarily consists of iron particles (from train wheels and rails), skin and hair cells, clothing fibers, and quartz silica (from brakes). Weight for weight, the health impact of underground dust is significantly less severe than that of cigarette smoke. Despite this, the comparison was widely misinterpreted and sensationalized. Media outlets, including the BBC and the London Evening Standard, reported that a 20-minute journey on the Northern Line was equivalent to smoking a cigarette. While technically true in terms of the weight of particulate matter inhaled, this statement misleadingly implied that the health effects were comparable, which is entirely false. This misrepresentation became an urban myth, repeated on various websites and even cited by the British Lung Foundation in 2003. The air quality in the London Underground is not ideal, particularly on the older deep tube lines like the Piccadilly, Northern, Bakerloo, and Central lines, which have the highest concentrations of particulates. Transport for London (TfL) and its predecessors have extensively studied the health impacts of underground air pollution. Detailed analyses of the dust composition have been conducted, but no definitive conclusions have been reached regarding its health effects. While the particulate concentrations are higher than desirable, the composition of the dust—mainly iron and skin cells—suggests it has a relatively low impact on human health compared to traffic exhaust or cigarette smoke. For those concerned about the health effects of breathing underground air, the 2005 paper by Seaton et al provides a balanced analysis of the issue. Additionally, the 2003 report by the Institute of Occupational Medicine offers a more detailed discussion of the topic.
